texts.label: text
texts.orig: Purpose: This systematic review presents cost-effectiveness studies of rotavirus vaccination in highincome settings based on dynamic transmission modelling to inform policy decisions about implementing rotavirus vaccination programmes.
texts.text: Purpose: This systematic review presents cost-effectiveness studies of rotavirus vaccination in highincome settings based on dynamic transmission modelling to inform policy decisions about implementing rotavirus vaccination programmes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Methods: We searched CEA Registry, MEDLINE, Embase, Health Technology Assessment Database, Scopus, and the National Health Service Economic Evaluation Database for studies published since 2002. Full economic evaluation studies based on dynamic transmission models, focusing on highincome countries, live oral rotavirus vaccine and children  5 years of age were eligible for inclusion. Included studies were appraised for quality and risk of bias using the Consensus on Health Economic Criteria (CHEC) list and the Philips checklist. The review protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO (CRD42020208406).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Results: A total of four economic evaluations were identified. Study settings included England and Wales, France, Norway, and the United States. All studies compared either pentavalent or monovalent rotavirus vaccines to no intervention. All studies were cost-utility analyses that reported incremental cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained. Included studies consistently concluded that rotavirus vaccination is cost-effective compared with no vaccination relative to the respective country's willingness to pay threshold when herd protection benefits are incorporated in the modelling framework.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Conclusions: Rotavirus vaccination was found to be cost-effective in all identified studies that used dynamic transmission models in high-income settings where child mortality rates due to rotavirus gastroenteritis are close to zero. Previous systematic reviews of economic evaluations considered mostly static models and had less conclusive findings than the current study. This review suggests that modelling choices influence cost-effectiveness results for rotavirus vaccination. Specifically, the review suggests that dynamic transmission models are more likely to account for the full impact of rotavirus vaccination than static models in cost-effectiveness analyses.

texts.text: 1. Introduction

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Rotavirus is a leading cause of severe diarrhoea and dehydration in children under five years of age [1]. It is transmitted through the oral-faecal route, with nearly all children infected by the age of five years [1]. In low- and middle-income countries, rotavirus infections are associated with high levels of child mortality [2]. In high income countries, while rotavirus-related mortality is rare, the disease is a significant cause of morbidity and imposes a substantial economic burden on societies and health systems [3] .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In 2009, Rotarix TM and RotaTeq TM were added to the World Health Organization (WHO) List of Essential Medicines [4]. However, rotavirus vaccination programmes have not been universally adopted, with 107 countries implementing vaccination programmes as of October 2020 [5]. As of 2016, only 45 % of highincome countries had introduced the vaccine [5]. Barriers to the implementation of universal rotavirus vaccination in highincome countries include poor knowledge among policy makers about the disease burden and its economic consequences, as well as a perception that rotavirus vaccination programmes are not cost-effective [6] .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Previously published systematic reviews have presented evidence relating to the cost-effectiveness of rotavirus vaccines in different income settings [3,7–10]. In 2009, Blicke and Beutels reviewed 18 economic evaluations of rotavirus vaccination programmes, nine of which were in developed countries, in order to describe and assess methodological and modelling choices [7] . The review reported that ''no unambiguous single answer emerged as to whether universal rotavirus vaccination is or is not costeffective" [7]. The study concluded that future research should account for herd protection using dynamic transmission models. In 2013, Aballéa et al. described key differences in methods, assumptions and inputs, which were influential in driving differences in conclusions [8]. Like Blicke and Beutels, the review recommended the use of dynamic transmission models to account for herd protection in order to capture the full economic value of rotavirus vaccination. In 2016, Thinboonboon et al. assessed the quality of evidence from economic evaluations [9]. The study identified significant variation in quality between low- and middle-income and high-income countries, which was attributed, in part, to a lack of capacity among low- and middle-income countries to conduct cost-effectiveness analyses with local researchers. In 2017, Koritum et al. provided a global overview of evidence relating to the costeffectiveness of rotavirus vaccines. The review included 104 studies, including 46 high-income countries, published between 2000 and 2015. 34 studies in high-income settings concluded rotavirus vaccination was cost-effective, whereas 12 concluded that rotavirus vaccination was not cost-effective [3]. In 2019, Haider et al. presented cost-effectiveness studies in low-income and lower- middle-income countries, concluding that rotavirus vaccination is cost-effective in those settings [10]. These systematic reviews have included mainly static models, such as Markov models and decision trees, which do not account for herd immunity. However, herd immunity effects have been consistently demonstrated in large observational studies worldwide, particularly in high-income settings where large database studies are possible and primary data collection studies are frequent [11–15] .

texts.orig: Four economic evaluations were identified from England and Wales, Norway, France, and the United States [20,21,23,24] (Table 4). Two models used variations of a susceptible-infectedrecovered (SIR) structure [23,24], while a third study featured a susceptible-exposed-infected-recovered (SEIR) structure [21]. texts.orig: All four studies were cost-utility analyses, which used qualityadjusted life years (QALYs) as the primary measurement for health-related quality of life, and compared vaccination versus no vaccination [20,21,23,24]. One study was conducted from the healthcare perspective only [20]. Two studies used a healthcare and societal perspective [21,23] and one study used a third-party payer and societal perspective [24]. The time-horizon was five years [21], 20 years [23] and 50 years [20,24]. All studies applied discount rates, which varied between 3 and 4 %. Three studies used probabilistic sensitivity analyses [20,21,24], while one study was unclear about the methods used for sensitivity analysis [23] .

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The cost per QALY gained ranged from cost-saving [20,21,23] to USD 192,100 [23] . Three studies found vaccination to be costeffective from the healthcare perspective [20,21,23] . Two papers reported that vaccination would be cost-saving from a societal perspective [21,23]. One paper concluded it would be cost-saving from a healthcare perspective if it was administered concomitantly with DTaP/IPV/Hib vaccines and under the assumption that vaccine efficacy does not begin to wane immediately after administration [20] .

texts.orig: 4. Discussion
texts.text: 4. Discussion

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This review identified four economic analyses that used dynamic transmission modelling to evaluate the costeffectiveness of rotavirus vaccination. Consistent with results of dynamic transmission models in previous systematic reviews, all included studies concluded that rotavirus vaccination was costeffective in high-income settings from both societal and healthcare perspectives when compared with no vaccination (see Table 5).
texts.text: This review identified four economic analyses that used dynamic transmission modelling to evaluate the costeffectiveness of rotavirus vaccination. Consistent with results of dynamic transmission models in previous systematic reviews, all included studies concluded that rotavirus vaccination was costeffective in high-income settings from both societal and healthcare perspectives when compared with no vaccination (see Table 5).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The impact of vaccine herd-protection effects in costeffectiveness analyses of childhood vaccination has been noted previously. Two systematic reviews on the cost-effectiveness of rotavirus vaccination have recommended that future economic evaluations use dynamic transmission models to account for herd immunity [7,8]; while a quantitative comparative analysis of childhood vaccinations published in 2017 concluded that ''when the target-vaccination strategy was not cost-saving without herdprotection, inclusion of herd-protection always resulted in more favourable results " [25]. Dynamic transmission modelling was also recommended in the WHO guide for standardization of economic evaluations of immunization programmes for infectious diseases that involve human to human transmission and where one of the eligible target groups includes an ''epidemiologically influential subgroup", such as children [26]. Still, as highlighted by this review, few economic evaluations have featured dynamic transmissionmodelling to determine the cost-effectiveness of rotavirus vaccination programmes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Static models that ignore herd immunity effects can underestimate the cost-effectiveness of vaccination and introduce structural bias against vaccinations for infectious diseases. Brisson et al. demonstrated that structural uncertainty, including modelling choices, could have equal or greater impacts on results than parameter uncertainty [27]. Of note, these assumptions and modelling choices are also rarely included in sensitivity analyses. Koritum et al. analysed eight cost-utility studies using static models, which compared universal rotavirus vaccination to no intervention in the United Kingdom, France, and the USA [3]. Out of the eight studies, six studies concluded that rotavirus vaccination was not cost-effective. Similarly, a report in 2009 featuring an economic evaluation using a static model in Norway concluded that rotavirus vaccination would not be cost-effective [28] .

texts.orig: Herd immunity effects after administration of rotavirus vaccine have been observed in the United States, Australia, Finland, and several other high-income countries where database studies are possible [11–15]. Following introduction of rotavirus vaccination, decreases in rotavirus incidence have been observed in children, adults, and the elderly. This is consistent with household transmission studies that demonstrated that rotavirus was highly transmissible within households, thus suggesting that averting cases in children potentially averts cases in older siblings and relatives [29–31]. Of note, post-licensure analyses and modelling of rotavirus vaccination in the United States, Australia, and Finland have suggested vaccination to be cost-saving, with Finnish postlicensure observational data indicating that for every fully vaccinated child there were 33 Euros (2015E) in savings from a health care payer perspective [32,33] .

Analyses for other diseases have dealt with this challenge by considering herd-immunity effects directly in Markov models [34]. Of note, a limitation of the current study is that it only looked at highincome settings. Post-licensure studies documenting herd immunity effects in low- and middle-income settings are scarce. Further studies are required to ascertain the magnitude of herd immunity effects in low- and middle-income countries, where rotavirus vaccines has been shown to be less effective.

Notably, included studies utilised different model types, including M  SEIR, SIR-V, M  SIR, while one study did not clearly define its model structure. Variation between model types could also result in structural biases that are likely to influence the results of each study. Increased standardisation and guidance for economic modelling would facilitate better comparisons across studies. Still, across all reviewed studies, rotavirus vaccination was consistently identified as a cost-effective intervention from both societal and health system perspectives, indicating the results are robust to variation in parameter and structural decisions within a dynamic transmission model framework.

texts.orig: 5. Conclusion
texts.text: 5. Conclusion

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This study identified four economic evaluations that concluded rotavirus vaccination was cost-effective from both societal and health system perspectives. These studies allowed for rotavirus vaccination to impact disease transmission and thus unvaccinated individuals, consistent with large observational studies in highincome countries. As shown in other systematic reviews, only a minority of models have taken herd immunity into account, possibly underestimating the cost-effectiveness of rotavirus vaccination in a way that cannot be captured via sensitivity analyses. Thus, dynamic transmission models remain the most adequate models to quantify the benefits of rotavirus vaccination in high-income countries, with static models providing only conservative estimates of the value of rotavirus vaccination.
